<reason>Both sides agreed distrust rose and the euro survived, so the debate turned on which was the larger residue. PRO (B) built the more concrete causal story (creditor-debtor morality tales, democratic bypass, distrust running in both directions, protest parties on both sides) and supplied an actual weighing threshold—durability—backed by plausible general knowledge (AfD becoming permanent, southern trust not recovering, seven years without deposit insurance or a budget, then a recovery fund built to look unlike the old playbook). CON (A) argued coherently that conditionality was what made the cheques politically possible and that the real counterfactual was contagion, but its metric drifted toward "nobody left plus instruments existed," which B pressed as near-unfalsifiable and then turned against A using A's own internment example (Greece 2015 had capital controls and threatened expulsion). A's "symmetric shock" reply on the pandemic fund was reasonable but did not fully dislodge B's point that the architects declined to reuse the method. B's claim that its questions were "answered by silence" before A had its answering turn was a real misstep, but B's closing engaged A's actual answers and the overall case for B remained clearer and easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing turn on A's own falsifiability answer: A said a euro held by capital controls, threatened expulsion, and no shared money would fail the motion; B noted Greece 2015 had the first two and argued the "cheques" were loans to repay foreign banks under terms voters had just rejected—a transfer of risk, not trust. Combined with the "seven years of nothing, then a design that repudiated the old one" durability point, it damaged A's central redefinition of solidarity.</best_rebuttal>
